weekly: Introduction to course goals and evaluation method; review of syllabus and course material. Fundamental question: WHO ARE WE, AND HOW DID WE GET HERE?
Darwin's ghosts - evolutionary thought before Darwin; 19th century revolutions and revelations; 20th century and beyond: The Hand of Man; genes in the space age.

weekly: 1a Introduction: What is archaeology? 1b History of Archaeology I: A playground for the wealthy. 1c History of Archaeology II: Archaeology, colonialism and nationalism.

2a History of Archaeology III: Archaeology and history - Deciphering languages. 2b Modern Archaeology as science I: Digging up the past. 2c Modern Archaeology as science II: The world around us - survey, landscape archaeology, remote sensing.

3a Modern Archaeology as science III: How old are the things we find? Dating in Archaeology. 3b Modern Archaeology as science IV: interpreting the past, the path from data to model. 3c Lucy and the beginning of the human story.
4a Java Man: enigmatic ancestors. 4b Altamira: the discovery of ancient creativity. 4c The cold case of Ötzi, a 5300-year-old homicide victim. Quiz 1
5a The Amesbury archer: discovering the people of famous places. 5b Crystallized in the past: the Hallstatt salt mines. 5c Bog Bodies: Northern European human sacrifices.
6a Sutton Hoo: unexpected treasures. 6b Richard III: the king in a parking lot. 6c Göbeklitepe: redefining our ideas about the prehistoric past.
Midterm
8a Çatalhöyük: peopling an empty landscape. 8b At the gates of Troy. 8c Hattusa, an imperial capital.
9a Ulu Burun, a mirror into ancient maritime trade. 9b At the court of the Mycenaean kings. 9c Knossos between legend and reality.
Quiz 2, presentations group 1
11a Antikythera: astonishing ancient technology. 11b Under the ashes: Pompeii and the Vesuvian eruption of 79 CE. 11c The Pyramids of Egypt: unravelling an ancient landscape.
12a The Amarna letters and the First Age of Diplomacy. 12b Tutankhamon: the most famous discovery ever? 12c The Nineveh reliefs and Assyrian politics of fear.
13a The Emperor’s eternal guards. 13b Templo Major: Aztecs, colonists and the ‘discovery’ of new worlds. 13c Custer’s ‘Last Stand’: mythmaking, indigenous peoples and setting the record straight.
Presentations group 2
textbooks: Required - Textbook: The Story of Archaeology , J.Pollard, 2007
outcomes: Explain how archaeology has changed our understanding of the past.
Discuss research advances in archaeological techniques and knowledge about the past.
Assess the value of archaeology in social terms.

weekly: Background: Roman imperial art and architecture. The rise of Christian art. The Catacombs of Rome; wall paintings of Dura Europus (Syria).
From Constantine to Theodosius (4th century). Architecture: Old St. Peter's (Rome) and the basilica. Church of the Holy Sepulchre (Jerusalem); Constantinople, the new imperial capital.

Pictorial art in the late 4th century: the Missorium of Theodosius I; the obelisk base in the hippodrome (Constantinople). Architecture, late 4th-5th centuries: Constantinople, Kanlı Divane, Alahan, and (in Syria) Qalat Seman.
Rome and Ravenna: architecture and art in the 5th-6th centuries.
Sixth century: the age of Justinian. Constantinople: Sts. Sergius & Bacchus, Hagia Sophia, Great Palace mosaic. Ravenna: San Vitale. Egypt (Sinai): St. Catherine's monastery.
Pictorial art: illustrated manuscripts, 4th-6th centuries. Iconoclasm (726-843).
Islamic art and architecture, 7th-13th centuries. The origins of Islamic art. Umayyad art and architecture (late 7th-mid 8th c.).
Abbasid art and architecture (mid 8th - 13th c.).
Midterm examination.
Contemporaries of the Abbasids: Muslim Spain; Fatimid Egypt; Iran and its neighbors.
Mİddle Byzantine art and architecture. Hosios Loukas. Illustrated manuscripts. The mosaics of Hagia Sophia.
Middle Byzantine church decoration: programs of mosaics and wall paintings. Hosios Loukas, Nea Moni (Chios), St. Sophia (Kiev), and Dafne (near Athens).
Byzantine influence in Venice, Norman Sicily, and the Balkans. Eastern neighbors: Armenians and Georgians.
Late Byzantine art and architecture. Kariye Camii (Constantinople).
